name: Battle of Thapsus
info: Julius Caesar's army defeated the Optimate forces of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio and King Juba I of Numidia near Thapsus in North Africa on 6 April 46 BCE, in the last civil war of the Roman Republic.

facts.place: Near Thapsus, beside the Marsh of Moknine, in the Roman province of Africa, in modern Tunisia
facts.sides: Julius Caesar, with twelve legions (five newly raised and seven veteran), a large number of archers and slingers and 3,000 to 5,000 cavalry, around 60,000 to 70,000 soldiers; the Optimates under Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio, with King Juba I of Numidia, eight Roman and three Numidian legions, 14,000 to 16,000 cavalry, about 20,000 light infantry and 60 elephants, around 90,000 soldiers in all
facts.outcome: Caesar's army won. The Optimate army broke and its camp was stormed. Scipio, Cato, Juba and Petreius died by their own hands soon afterwards, though the civil war went on in Hispania.

t: Caesar fought with a smaller army than his opponents: about 60,000 to 70,000 soldiers against around 90,000, who also had 60 elephants.
The elephants decided much of the fighting. Archers on Caesar's right drove those opposite them back into their own men, and the veterans of Legio V held the charge on his left.

Caesar's soldiers killed around ten thousand of the enemy after the battle, in spite of his repeated orders to spare them. The battle is generally regarded as the last large-scale use of war elephants in the West.
dyk: After the battle Legio V Alaudae is said to have been awarded an elephant as its symbol, because five of its cohorts had sustained the charge of the elephants on Caesar's left.
ev: Caesar crosses the Rubicon with the 13th Legion and the last civil war of the Republic begins
Caesar's foraging force is nearly overcome by Petreius and Labienus near Ruspina but withdraws to the town
Caesar besieges Thapsus and Scipio marches round the Marsh of Moknine to meet him
Caesar's army defeats the Optimate army at Thapsus
Cato kills himself at Utica, and Juba and Petreius die in a duel

sections.background:
The last civil war of the Roman Republic began in 49 BCE, when Caesar defied senatorial orders to disband his army after the war in Gaul. He crossed the Rubicon with the 13th Legion, in violation of Roman law, and marched on Rome. The Optimates fled to Greece under Pompey. Caesar followed and was defeated at Dyrrhachium, but recovered and beat Pompey at Pharsalus. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was assassinated.

The remaining Optimates, not ready to give up, regrouped in the African provinces. Their leaders were Cato the Younger and Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio. Other figures from the nobility in the resistance were Titus Labienus, Publius Attius Varus, Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius and Pompey's sons Sextus and Gnaeus. King Juba I of Numidia was a valuable local ally. After the pacification of the Eastern provinces and a short visit to Rome, Caesar followed his opponents to Africa.

He had gathered six legions around Lilybaeum in Sicily, with four more on their way from Rome. Despite poor weather he sailed and reached the African coast on 28 December, landing near Hadrumetum. A storm had scattered his transports, leaving him with just 3,000 infantry and 150 cavalry. Hadrumetum was held by a strong garrison, and Caesar found he had neither the men nor the materiel to take it. Warned that a large force of enemy cavalry was coming, he marched south, harassed by Numidian light cavalry, and reached Ruspina on 29 December.
sections.forces:
Caesar had twelve legions at Thapsus: five newly raised ones (XXV, XXVI, XXVIII, XXIX and XXX) and seven veteran ones (V, VII, VIII, IX, X, XIII and XIV). The veteran legions had campaigned for many years and were all understrength. He also had a large number of archers and slingers and 3,000 to 5,000 cavalry, so that he had around 60,000 to 70,000 soldiers when he arrived at Thapsus.

The Optimates had eight Roman and three Numidian legions, around 55,000 legionaries, with 14,000 to 16,000 cavalry, about 20,000 light infantry and 60 elephants. Their army totalled around 90,000 soldiers. Earlier in the campaign Juba's arrival had brought their force up to thirteen legions, and Scipio had refused to attack Caesar's positions.

Scipio drew up his legions in three lines in the centre, with cavalry and light infantry on the flanks and the elephants in front of the flanks. Caesar also formed three lines: Legio VII and X on the right, VIII and IX on the left, and XIII and XIV in the centre with a newly recruited legion on either side of them, mixing recruits and veterans being one of his trademarks. His slingers, archers and cavalry stood on the flanks, and Legio V, split in two, was held in reserve behind the flanks to counter the elephants. Caesar commanded the right. He had left two recently recruited legions to continue the siege of the city.
sections.course:
In February Caesar arrived at Thapsus and besieged it, surrounding it with a double line of circumvallation. The Marsh of Moknine left two landward approaches. Caesar fortified the southern one with three cohorts, forcing his opponents to attack it or march round the marsh to the east. Scipio chose the second and placed Afranius and a few soldiers opposite the fortifications and Juba and Labienus with the Numidian cavalry south of the marsh. The main army marched to the eastern approach and began building a camp, covered by the rest of the army drawn up in battle formation.

Neither side committed to battle for some time. Then a trumpeter of the VII sounded the attack, and Caesar, seeing his right surge forward, ordered a general advance. His archers on the right attacked the elephants opposite them, which panicked and trampled their own men. On the other flank the elephants charged Caesar's left. His light infantry and cavalry moved out of their path, and five cohorts of Legio V Alaudae, placed behind the flank, sustained the charge, stabbing their pila at the elephants' eyes and weak spots and sounding their trumpets until the beasts ran back into their own right flank.

After the loss of the elephants Scipio began to lose ground, his left broke first and the rest followed. Caesar's cavalry outmanoeuvred its enemy and destroyed the fortified camp. The garrison of Thapsus sallied out against the siege works but was forced back by the two legions Caesar had left there, which marched south and overran Afranius's camp. Juba's allied troops abandoned the site before they could attack the Numidians.
sections.aftermath:
Caesar went on to the Optimates' camp and found it already stormed. There he lost control of his own men, who began slaughtering their opponents. Around ten thousand enemies were killed, those who survived the battle being put to the sword by soldiers who ignored Caesar's repeated orders to spare them. Plutarch reports that according to some sources Caesar had an epileptic seizure just before he ordered his lines forward, causing confusion and disobeyed orders.

Scipio, Labienus, Juba, Afranius and Petreius escaped from the field. Labienus, with Sextus Pompeius and Varus, fled to Gnaeus Pompeius, who was raising forces on the Iberian Peninsula. Afranius and Faustus Cornelius Sulla collected survivors and began to pillage eastern Mauretania, whose king had sided with Caesar, but were caught by Publius Sittius, a mercenary commander working for King Bocchus II and an ally of Caesar, and executed a few days later. Juba and Petreius fled to Numidia, and with Sittius closing in they chose to die by duelling each other. According to De Bello Africo, Juba killed Petreius and then had a slave kill him.

Caesar renewed the siege of Thapsus, which eventually fell, and went on to Utica, where Cato was garrisoned. On news of the defeat Cato killed himself. Plutarch reports that Caesar said, "Cato, I must grudge you your death, as you grudged me the honour of saving your life." Scipio tried to reach Hispania with a small fleet, but bad weather drove him back to the African coast, where Sittius and his fleet caught him off Hippo Regius. After losing the naval engagement, Scipio stabbed himself with his sword.
sections.sources:
The battle is known in part from De Bello Africo, a Latin work continuing Caesar's accounts of his campaigns against his Republican enemies in the province of Africa. It is the source for the deaths of Juba and Petreius in their duel. Plutarch supplies two further reports: that according to some sources Caesar had an epileptic seizure just before he ordered his lines forward, causing confusion and disobeyed orders, and the remark Caesar made on hearing of Cato's death.

Estimates of both armies' strengths are round ranges, 60,000 to 70,000 for Caesar and around 90,000 for the Optimates, and the ten thousand enemy dead is a single round figure. The seizure is reported only as the view of some sources, and it is one explanation offered for the slaughter that Caesar could not stop.
sections.legacy:
The battle brought peace to Africa. Caesar left and returned to Rome on 25 July of the same year. The Optimate cause was not finished, since Labienus, the sons of Pompey, Varus and several others gathered another army in Baetica in Hispania Ulterior. The civil war was not over, and the Battle of Munda was to follow.

The deaths of Scipio and Cato, of Juba and Petreius, and of Afranius and Faustus Cornelius Sulla removed most of the leadership that had held the African provinces against Caesar. Caesar is reported by Plutarch to have been upset at Cato's suicide.

The Battle of Thapsus is generally regarded as marking the last large-scale use of war elephants in the West. Legio V Alaudae was awarded an elephant as its symbol for its stand against them.

summary: At Thapsus on 6 April 46 BCE Caesar's twelve legions routed the Optimate army of Scipio and King Juba of Numidia, said to number around 90,000, after the elephants panicked. Scipio, Cato, Juba and Petreius killed themselves soon after, but the civil war went on in Hispania.
notes: Article says 'defeated in the Battle of Dyrrhachium' for Caesar's Populares: left as 'defeated at Dyrrhachium'. Its sentence that the Optimates 'regrouped in the African provinces of Mauretania' is odd (Africa and Numidia, not only Mauretania): written as 'African provinces'.
Caesar's 'Populares' and 'Optimates' labels used as the article uses them for the Optimate side only.

'Around ten thousand killed' is the article's figure for enemies killed; it does not say whether this includes losses during the fighting or only those after it. I wrote 'killed after the battle' in the takeaway and aftermath; the editor should check whether 'after' overstates it (the article says 'those surviving the battle being put to the sword').
The 'dyk' and legacy claim that Legio V was awarded an elephant rests on the article's 'afterwards the legion was awarded an elephant as a symbol'; I hedged with 'is said to' in the dyk only.
The date: article says April 6, 46 BC (Julian calendar not discussed). The Caesar's return date 25 July is the article's.
Left out: Hadrumetum garrison commanders' names, the Ruspina fighting details, the Uzitta episode, torture of captives, Gaetulian defections, Cercina grain capture, and the Sallust admiral.
Article says Caesar's seven legions at one point and 'twelve legions' at Thapsus; consistent.
ev dates carry no year where the article gives none (landing 'December', Ruspina 'January', Thapsus siege 'February'); the article says only '28 December' and does not state 47 BCE.
Sources section is short: the article names only De Bello Africo and Plutarch and no historian's dispute.
